q: When was the US created?
answer: The United States is usually dated to July 4, 1776. That's the day the Second Continental Congress, meeting in Philadelphia, adopted the Declaration of Independence, which is why July 4 is celebrated as Independence Day [1][2]. Delegates didn't start signing the document until August 2, 1776 [2]. There are other milestones too. Britain recognized American independence in the Treaty of Paris in 1783. The Constitutional Convention adopted the current Constitution on September 17, 1787. It was ratified in June 1788, and the federal government began operating under it on March 4, 1789 [3]. So the nation dates from 1776, but the current form of government started in 1789.

q: What was the goal of the French Revolution?
answer:
The French Revolution (1789–1799) didn't have one fixed goal. Its aims grew more radical over time. Broadly, revolutionaries wanted to tear down the "Ancien Régime," the absolute monarchy that gave special privileges to the nobility and the Catholic clergy. In its place they wanted a system built on Enlightenment ideas: popular sovereignty, citizenship, equal rights before the law, and fair taxation [1][2].

These ideas were summed up in the motto "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity." Liberty meant freedom from arbitrary rule. Equality meant ending feudal privileges and tax exemptions. Fraternity meant uniting the French people as one nation [2]. The early achievements show what the revolutionaries were after. The August 1789 decrees abolished feudalism and the church tithe. The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen set out basic rights. The first plan was a constitutional monarchy that limited the king's power [1].

After that, goals changed with circumstances. Pressure from war, economic crisis and radical groups such as the Jacobins led to the monarchy being abolished and the First Republic declared in September 1792, and Louis XVI was executed in 1793. Then came the Reign of Terror, the Thermidorian Reaction and the Directory [1].

So the short answer is that it began as an effort to fix France's finances and limit royal and aristocratic privilege. It ended up trying to rebuild French society around rights, equality and the nation.

q: Who really created the foundation of electricity?
answer:
No one person created it. Electricity is a natural phenomenon, so it was discovered bit by bit over centuries rather than invented [2]. If you want one name for the foundation, it's usually William Gilbert, the English physician who is often called the "father of electricity." In his book De Magnete (1600) he studied static attraction in a systematic way and coined the Latin word "electricus," meaning "amber-like." That word gave us "electricity," and the book also introduced terms like "electric force" and "magnetic pole" [1][3].

Others built on that work. The ancient Greek Thales of Miletus noticed static effects from rubbing amber much earlier. Stephen Gray showed the difference between conductors and insulators, and the Leyden jar (1745) made it possible to store charge. Benjamin Franklin showed that lightning is electrical, which is why he's often the name people give [2]. Alessandro Volta built the first battery in 1800, the first steady source of current [3]. Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831, the principle behind the electric generator [3]. James Clerk Maxwell later combined electricity and magnetism into a single theory. Edison and Tesla came after all of this; they turned the science into practical power systems rather than laying its foundations [2].

So the fairest answer is Gilbert for the scientific starting point, and Faraday and Maxwell for the physics that makes modern electrical power possible.

q: Why is the sky blue and not green?
answer:
Sunlight is scattered by air molecules through Rayleigh scattering, and the amount of scattering rises steeply as wavelength gets shorter (roughly as 1/wavelength⁴). Blue light is scattered about 10 times more than red [1][2]. Green is in the middle of the spectrum, so it gets scattered more than red but clearly less than blue and violet. Nothing in the process favors green in particular, so the light coming from the sky is a broad mix that leans heavily toward the short, blue end.

By that logic you might expect a violet sky. It isn't violet for two reasons. The Sun puts out less violet than blue, and ozone high in the atmosphere absorbs some of the violet that does arrive. Our eyes are also less sensitive to violet [1][2]. When that mixed skylight reaches the eye, the blue-sensitive cones are stimulated most. The green-sensitive and red-sensitive cones respond more weakly, and the combination looks like pale blue rather than green or violet [2].

For the sky to look green, the scattered light would need to peak in the middle of the spectrum. Rayleigh scattering doesn't produce that.

q: How does a motor work?
answer:
I'll assume you mean an electric motor. Most electric motors work because a wire carrying current inside a magnetic field feels a push, called the Lorentz force. The motor arranges this so the push turns the shaft [1]. The force is strongest when the current and the magnetic field cross at right angles, and it pushes in a direction perpendicular to both [2].

In a simple DC motor, a coil of wire sits between magnets. Current goes one way along one side of the loop and the opposite way along the other, so one side gets pushed up and the other down, and the loop twists. On its own, the loop would just rock back and forth around a resting position. To prevent that, a split-ring commutator turns with the coil, and stationary brushes press against it. Every half turn, the brushes switch to the other segment, which reverses the current in the coil. Because of that switch, the push always turns the coil the same way, so it keeps spinning [3][4].

Other designs use the same idea and just flip the current differently. Brushless motors switch the current electronically instead of using brushes. AC induction motors use alternating current to create a magnetic field that rotates, and that field drags the rotor around with it [1]. If you meant a gasoline "motor" (an internal combustion engine), that works on a completely different principle: burning fuel pushes pistons.

q: How does 3D printing work?
answer:
3D printing, also called additive manufacturing, builds an object by adding material one thin layer at a time from a digital design [1]. You start with a 3D model, usually made in CAD software and saved in a format like STL. Software called a slicer cuts that model into hundreds or thousands of horizontal slices and works out the path the printer should follow for each one [1]. The printer then makes the part slice by slice, bonding each new layer to the one below it, until the full object is finished.

How each layer gets made depends on the technology. The most common method for home printers is fused deposition modeling (FDM, also called fused filament fabrication). It feeds plastic filament from a spool through a heated nozzle, which moves around and lays down melted plastic that hardens as it cools, much like a very precise hot-glue gun [1][2]. Stereolithography (SLA) uses a vat of liquid resin that hardens under light. A UV laser traces each layer so the resin solidifies exactly where it hits [1][2]. Selective laser sintering (SLS) spreads a thin layer of fine powder, usually nylon, and uses a laser to fuse the parts that belong to the object. The loose powder around it holds the part up, so SLS doesn't need the temporary support structures that FDM and SLA often do for overhangs [1][3]. There are other methods too, such as metal powder-bed fusion and inkjet-style material jetting, but they all follow the same basic idea of building up layers from a digital file.

q: How can an airplane be so fast?
answer:
A few things work together. First, jet engines are extremely powerful. They push huge amounts of air and hot gas out the back very fast, and by Newton's third law the plane gets pushed forward [1]. Second, once a plane is cruising, the engines don't have to hold it up, because the wings make lift that balances the weight. The engines only need to overcome air resistance (drag). When thrust equals drag, the plane holds a steady speed [1]. Third, airliners cruise very high, usually around 31,000–38,000 ft (9,400–11,600 m) [2]. The air up there is much thinner, so drag at a given speed is much lower [3]. That's why a modern jet like the 787 or A350 can cruise at about Mach 0.85, roughly 900 km/h (560 mph) [2].

Their smooth, streamlined shape helps too, and so does the fact that there's no road or wheel friction in the air. They don't go even faster because drag climbs sharply as they approach the speed of sound, which makes flying faster costly in fuel. Airliners are designed to cruise just below that point.

q: Why are people saying WiFi and radio waves are harmful? What is the evidence?
answer:
Most of the worry comes from a few real findings that often get stretched. The strong evidence, though, doesn't show that WiFi or phones harm people at normal exposure levels.

**Where the concern comes from**
- **A 2011 WHO classification.** The WHO's cancer agency (IARC) labeled radiofrequency radiation "possibly carcinogenic" (Group 2B) [1]. That's its weakest positive category. It means the evidence was limited and couldn't be ruled out, not that harm was shown.
- **A US rat study.** The US National Toxicology Program found "clear evidence" of a rare heart tumor (malignant schwannoma) in male rats given whole-body exposure, and "some evidence" of brain gliomas [2][3]. The rats got high doses for many hours a day over their whole lives, so it's hard to apply the results to how people use phones.
- **Recent US politics.** In January 2026, HHS started a new study of cellphone and wireless radiation, and the FDA took down webpages that had called cellphone radiation safe [4][5]. Some people took that as an admission of danger. What changed was the policy, not the science.

**What the stronger evidence shows**
- **Cancer.** In 2024 the WHO commissioned a large review of human studies. It found moderate-certainty evidence that mobile phone use likely doesn't raise the risk of brain tumors (glioma, meningioma, acoustic neuroma) in adults or children. It found the same for childhood leukemia and exposure from cell towers and other transmitters [1][6]. Some researchers dispute it, arguing it underplays higher risks among the heaviest, longest-term users [7].
- **Physics.** Radio waves are "non-ionizing," meaning they don't carry enough energy to break chemical bonds or damage DNA the way X-rays or UV light can. The main proven effect is slight heating, and exposure limits are set well below that.
- **Electromagnetic hypersensitivity.** Some people say WiFi gives them headaches or other symptoms, and the WHO accepts that those symptoms are real [8]. But in double-blind tests, these people couldn't tell when a real field was switched on. They reported symptoms just as often after fake exposures [9].

**Bottom line:** The FDA, CDC and FCC have long held that phone radiation within legal limits is safe, and large population studies haven't found a clear cancer link [4]. There are still open questions, like very heavy lifetime use and newer technologies such as 5G. But the claim that WiFi is harmful goes well beyond what the evidence supports.

q: Who created the concept of the government?
answer:
Nobody created government. It developed gradually in many places, and no one knows exactly when it began. After farming spread in the Neolithic Revolution, food surpluses let some people take on jobs other than farming, including ruling. The first small city-states appeared about 5,000 years ago. Larger governed areas followed in the third and second millennia BC: Sumer, ancient Egypt, the Indus Valley and the Yellow River civilizations [1]. Sumer is often named as the earliest example. Priests and councils first ran its city-states, and kingship had emerged by about 3600 BCE, though scholars still argue over how and when it started [2].

If you mean who first wrote theories about government, the classic answer is the ancient Greeks. Plato's *Republic* (around 375 BC) sorted governments into five types, from aristocracy down to tyranny. Aristotle's *Politics* grouped them by whether one person, a few or the many hold power [1]. Later, Thomas Hobbes argued there could be only three kinds of commonwealth: monarchy, aristocracy and democracy [1].

q: How does an oven work?
answer:
Most home ovens are insulated metal boxes that heat up with either gas or electricity [1]. In an electric oven, current runs through heating elements made of high-resistance wire, usually nichrome, which get hot. This is called Joule heating. The glowing elements give off infrared radiation that heats the air, the oven walls and the food [2][3]. A gas oven does the same job by burning natural gas or bottled gas at a burner, usually at the bottom of the oven [1].

A thermostat keeps the temperature steady. A sensor in the oven checks the temperature, and the controls turn the heat off when the oven reaches the setting and back on when it cools below it. That's why the element or burner cycles on and off while you cook [3][1]. The food heats in three ways: radiation from the elements and hot walls, hot air moving around it, and conduction through the pan. A convection oven adds a fan, usually at the back, that pushes the hot air around. This gets rid of hot and cold spots and usually cooks faster and more evenly [4][1]. Microwave ovens work differently: they use microwaves to heat the water molecules inside the food directly [1].

q: What's the difference between a crocodile and an alligator?
answer:
Crocodiles and alligators are related, but they belong to separate families: Crocodylidae and Alligatoridae. The simplest way to tell them apart is the snout. Alligators have a broad, rounded U-shaped snout, while crocodiles have a longer, narrower V-shaped one [1]. Teeth are another clue. An alligator's upper jaw is wider than its lower jaw, so when its mouth is closed you mostly see the upper teeth. A crocodile's upper and lower teeth line up and stay visible, especially a large fourth tooth on each side of the lower jaw [1][2].

There's also a difference inside the body. Crocodiles have salt glands on the tongue that work well, so they can live in brackish water and even salt water. Alligators' salt glands work poorly, so they mostly stay in fresh water [1]. That helps explain where they live. There are only two alligator species, one in the southeastern U.S. and one in China. Crocodiles live across the tropics in Africa, Asia, Australia and the Americas. South Florida is the one place where both live side by side. Alligators also tend to be darker, almost black, while crocodiles are usually a lighter olive or tan [2].

q: How can you tell a leopard, a jaguar and a cheetah apart?
answer:
Start with the coat. A cheetah has solid, round black spots scattered evenly over its body. Leopards and jaguars have rosettes, which are rings of spots around a lighter centre. A leopard's rosettes are smaller and have nothing inside them. A jaguar's are bigger and usually have one or more small dots in the middle [1][2].

Next, check the face. Only the cheetah has black "tear lines" running from the inner corners of its eyes down to its mouth [1][2].

Body shape helps too. The cheetah is a lean, long-legged sprinter with a small, rounded head. The leopard is more compact and muscular. The jaguar is the heaviest of the three, with a broad head, a powerful jaw and a fairly short tail.

Location settles most cases. Jaguars live only in the Americas, while leopards and cheetahs live in Africa and Asia [2]. So a spotted big cat in South America is a jaguar. Keep in mind that "black panthers" are just dark-coated leopards or jaguars, and in good light you can often still see their rosettes.

q: How is Buddhism different from Hinduism?
answer:
Both religions come from ancient India and share a lot of vocabulary: karma, rebirth, samsara (the cycle of birth and death), dharma, and the goal of getting free from that cycle, called moksha in Hinduism and nirvana in Buddhism [1]. They differ mainly on the points below.

- **Origins and scripture:** Buddhism goes back to one founder, the Buddha, in about the 5th century BCE. Hinduism has no single founder and grew out of Vedic religion blended with other Indian traditions. Buddhism rejected the authority of the Vedas and Upanishads, which Hinduism treats as sacred [1][2].
- **The self:** Hinduism teaches that each person has an eternal soul (atman). Buddhism's "not-self" (anatta) teaching says there's no permanent self, only five constantly changing parts: body, feelings, perception, mental formations and consciousness [1][2].
- **God and ultimate reality:** Hinduism describes Brahman as the eternal source of everything, and many traditions worship a supreme God. Buddhism doesn't rely on a creator God or on Brahman. It explains reality through "dependent arising," the idea that everything comes into being because of other conditions [1].
- **Caste:** Hinduism historically built the caste system into its social and religious order. The Buddha taught that caste doesn't matter for spiritual progress [1][2].

Keep in mind that "Hinduism" covers a wide range of schools, so any short comparison simplifies things.

q: What's the difference between baking soda and baking powder?
answer:
Both are chemical leaveners, and the difference comes down to acid. Baking soda is pure sodium bicarbonate, a base. It only makes carbon dioxide bubbles when it meets an acidic ingredient in the recipe, like buttermilk, yogurt, vinegar, lemon juice, brown sugar, molasses or natural cocoa. It starts reacting as soon as the two touch [1][2]. Baking powder is sodium bicarbonate that already has a dry acid mixed in, plus a filler such as cornstarch to keep the two apart. It only needs liquid to start working [2][3].

Most store-bought baking powder is "double-acting." It contains one acid that reacts when the batter gets wet and a second that reacts in the heat of the oven. That second rise makes baked goods fluffier and means the batter doesn't have to go into the oven right away [2][3]. Recipes with a lot of acid often call for both. For example, one cup of flour with one cup of buttermilk might use ½ teaspoon baking powder plus ¼ teaspoon baking soda, instead of a full teaspoon of baking powder [3].

You can't swap one for the other one-to-one. If you use baking soda without enough acid, the result won't rise properly and can taste soapy or metallic.

q: What's the difference between a virus and a bacterium, and why don't antibiotics work on viruses?
answer:
A bacterium is a complete single-celled living organism. It has a cell wall, its own ribosomes for making proteins, and its own metabolism, so it can grow and divide by itself, whether inside your body or out in the environment [1][2]. A virus is much smaller and isn't a cell at all. It's just genetic material (DNA or RNA) packed in a protein shell called a capsid, sometimes with an outer envelope. It can only copy itself by getting inside a host cell and using that cell's machinery [1][2][3].

That difference is why antibiotics don't work on viruses. Antibiotics attack parts found only in bacteria, like the bacterial cell wall, bacterial ribosomes, or enzymes bacteria need to copy their DNA. A virus has none of those, so there's nothing for the drug to hit [2][3][4]. Because a virus runs on your own cells' machinery, a drug that blocked that machinery would also harm you. Viral infections are instead handled by your immune system, vaccines, or antiviral drugs that target specific viral steps, such as Tamiflu for flu or HIV medicines [1][4]. Taking antibiotics for a viral illness like a cold doesn't help, can cause side effects, and helps create antibiotic-resistant bacteria [4][5].

q: How do Linux and Windows handle file permissions differently?
answer:
Linux and Windows both control who can use a file, but they are built differently. Classic Linux permissions are simple. Every file has one owner and one group, and three sets of read, write and execute (rwx) permissions: one for the owner, one for the group, and one for everyone else ("others"). You set these with chmod and chown [1][2]. Linux checks only the first category you fall into, in the order owner, group, others. Three special flags change the rules: setuid makes a program run as its owner, setgid makes new files in a folder take the folder's group, and the sticky bit stops people deleting other users' files in a shared folder [1].

Windows, on NTFS, uses an access control list (ACL) on each file. This is a list of entries, and each one names a user or group and lists the rights it is allowed or denied. There can be as many entries as you need, and the rights are much finer than read, write and execute [3][1]. Windows reads the entries in order until the requested access is either fully allowed or explicitly denied. Permissions usually pass down automatically from parent folders, and a separate list can log access attempts for auditing [3][1]. A file with no list at all is open to everyone, while a file with an empty list blocks everyone [3].

In short, Linux's model is easier to read and manage, and Windows's is more flexible but can get complicated once inheritance and deny rules pile up [2]. The difference is smaller than it looks, because Linux file systems like ext4 also support add-on POSIX ACLs (managed with setfacl and getfacl) that give named users and groups their own permissions [1].

q: What was the goal of Martin Luther and what happened to Christianity through his works?
answer:
Luther wanted to reform the Catholic Church, not break away from it. In 1517 he wrote the Ninety-five Theses to start an academic debate about the sale of indulgences, which he saw as an abuse. At first he intended to fix the Church from the inside [1][2]. At the heart of his theology was the belief that people are saved by God's grace through faith alone, not by good works or by buying Church remissions of sin [2][3].

His ideas didn't reform the Church the way he hoped. They split it instead. Pope Leo X excommunicated him in January 1521, and later that year Emperor Charles V declared him an outlaw at the Diet of Worms [3]. His writings helped spark the Protestant Reformation, which permanently divided Western Christianity into Roman Catholic and Protestant branches. His own teachings became the basis of Lutheranism [1][3]. His German translation of the Bible, completed in 1534, also made scripture much easier for ordinary people to read [3].

q: What technology is attributed to the foundation of AI and where did it start?
answer:
The technology usually credited as AI's foundation is the programmable digital computer. When scientists got access to these machines in the mid-1950s, some realized that a machine that could manipulate numbers could also manipulate symbols, and that manipulating symbols might be the essence of human thought [1].

AI as a formal field of research started at the Dartmouth Summer Research Project, a workshop held at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire, in the summer of 1956 [1][2]. It was organized by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester of IBM and Claude Shannon of Bell Labs. McCarthy had coined the term "artificial intelligence" in 1955 while proposing the workshop [2]. At the event, Allen Newell and Herbert Simon presented the Logic Theorist program. The workshop is widely considered the birth of AI, because it gave the field its name, its mission and its first major success [1].

The idea of thinking machines is much older than 1956. But if you mean the key technology and the place where the field began, the answer is the digital computer and Dartmouth.

q: How did the printing press help the Protestant Reformation spread?
answer:
The printing press let Reformation ideas travel faster and farther than church authorities could stop them. Luther's Ninety-five Theses (1517) were reprinted without his permission and spread across Germany within about two weeks [1]. By around 1520 he was Europe's most published author. Printers turned out 291 editions of his 45 original works, and about 300,000 copies circulated between 1518 and 1520 [2].

Reformers relied on short, cheap pamphlets written in German, called Flugschriften, which usually ran four to eight pages [2]. People often read them aloud in taverns and homes, so even people who couldn't read heard the arguments [3]. The same technology let Luther's German translation of the Bible reach ordinary readers. Later, where Protestant preaching was suppressed, pamphlets, broadsheets and secret printing became the main way Reformed ideas reached the public [2].

Economic historians have found that cities with printing presses by 1500 were noticeably more likely to become Protestant by 1530–1560. Scholars still debate how much of that was due to print itself and how much to trade routes and personal networks that went along with it [2].

q: Beethoven went deaf — how did he keep composing, and which famous works came after?
answer:
Beethoven kept composing because he could hear music in his head. He had been a trained professional musician since childhood, so he could imagine pitches, harmonies and whole textures without playing them. He also worked out his ideas on paper in sketchbooks, rather than needing to hear them played [3][1]. His hearing started to fail around 1798, when he was in his late twenties. In 1802 he wrote the Heiligenstadt Testament, a letter to his brothers that was never sent. In it he admitted he had thought about suicide but said he was determined to keep making music [2]. By the 1820s he was almost completely deaf. Visitors wrote their side of a conversation in "conversation books" and he answered out loud, sometimes jotting musical sketches in the same books [1][4]. One often-repeated story says he bit a rod touching the piano to feel the vibrations through his jaw, but that's hard to verify.

His deafness mostly ended his career as a performing pianist, not as a composer [2]. Nearly all his most famous works came after it began. From the middle years there are the "Eroica" (Third) and Fifth Symphonies and his only opera, Fidelio. From the late period there are the "Hammerklavier" and other late piano sonatas, the Missa solemnis, the late string quartets and the Ninth Symphony, which premiered in 1824 [2][3]. At that premiere, a well-known story says one of the singers had to turn him around so he could see the audience clapping, because he couldn't hear it.

q: Is it safe to drink tap water in Mexico City?

For practical purposes, drink bottled or purified water, and don't swallow water in pools or lakes [1]. Brushing your teeth with bottled water is the cautious choice too. Ice and drinks at established restaurants are generally made with purified water, but if in doubt, ask.

q: What should I do if I get stung by a jellyfish?
answer:
Get out of the water and rinse the sting with seawater, not fresh water. Fresh water can make stinging cells that are still on the skin fire more venom [1][2]. Lift off any tentacles you can see with a stick, a card, tweezers or a gloved hand, not bare fingers, and don't rub the area [2][3].

For pain, heat works better than cold. Soak the area in water that's hot but doesn't burn, about 40–45°C (104–113°F), for around 20 minutes or longer. A hot shower or hot pack also works [1][3]. Ibuprofen or acetaminophen can help with pain afterward [2]. Skip urine, alcohol and ammonia, which don't work and can make things worse [1][3].

Whether to use vinegar depends on the species. It's the standard treatment for box jellyfish stings, which are common in tropical Australia and the Indo-Pacific. But it can make Portuguese man o' war stings worse, and those are common in U.S. waters. So follow local lifeguard or beach signage advice on vinegar [2][3].

Call emergency services right away if the person has trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion or severe swelling. Also call if the sting covers a large area, or if it could be from a box jellyfish or Irukandji jellyfish.

q: What are the signs of altitude sickness, and how do I avoid it when hiking in Peru?
answer:
Altitude sickness (acute mountain sickness, or AMS) feels a lot like a hangover. The main sign is a headache, plus at least one of: loss of appetite, nausea or vomiting, dizziness, fatigue or poor sleep. It usually starts 2 to 12 hours after you arrive at altitude [1]. The dangerous forms need urgent action. Confusion, stumbling or clumsy walking, and unusual drowsiness can mean fluid on the brain (HACE). Severe breathlessness even at rest, chest congestion, or a cough that may bring up pink or bloody sputum can mean fluid in the lungs (HAPE). With either one, go down right away, at least 300 m, and use oxygen if it's available [1].

This matters in Peru because you usually fly straight into Cusco at about 3,400 m (11,150 ft). Flying directly to that height can make up to half of travelers sick [2]. On the classic Inca Trail, the high point is Dead Woman's Pass at 4,215 m (13,828 ft), and people most often get sick on the day 2 climb up to it [3].

To avoid it:
- Go slowly. Acclimatization takes 3 to 5 days, and it helps to spend a few days around 2,500 to 2,750 m first [2]. Many travelers do this in the lower Sacred Valley, which is a bit under 3,000 m. At minimum, spend 2 to 3 days in Cusco before any hard hiking [3].
- Follow the ascent rule on multi-day treks. Above 3,000 m, don't raise the height where you sleep by more than about 500 m per day, and add a rest night for every 1,000 m you gain [1].
- Take it easy at first. Keep activity light for the first day or two and skip alcohol for 48 hours [1].
- Ask a doctor about acetazolamide (Diamox) before you go. It speeds up acclimatization and is usually started the day before you go up [1][2].
- Don't push through symptoms. If they get worse, stop climbing, and if they get much worse, go down.

q: When is the best time to visit Iceland to see the northern lights?
answer:
The aurora season in Iceland runs from about late September to early April. That's when the nights are long and dark enough to see it; from May to August the midnight sun makes it practically impossible [1][2]. The months on either side of the equinoxes, late September to October and February to March, are often named the best. These months tend to have more geomagnetic activity, and the weather in them is usually less harsh than midwinter [3][2]. February is often picked as the single best month because it combines long nights with fairly settled weather [3]. By April, Reykjavík only gets about five hours of real darkness a night, so your chances drop [3]. On any given night, the best viewing is usually between about 9 pm and 2 am [3].

Whatever month you choose, three things have to happen together: darkness, solar activity and clear skies. Cloud cover is usually the real obstacle in Iceland. To improve your odds, plan several nights, get away from city lights, try to avoid the days around a full moon, and check the Icelandic Met Office's aurora and cloud forecast each day [3][1].

q: What vaccinations do I need for a trip to Kenya?
answer:
The only vaccine Kenya can make you show proof of at entry is yellow fever, and only in certain cases. If you fly directly from the US or Canada, you don't need it. You do need a yellow fever certificate if you're arriving from a country with yellow fever risk, or if you spend more than 12 hours in an airport in one of those countries on the way [1][2].

Even when it isn't required, the CDC recommends the yellow fever shot for everyone aged 9 months or older. The exceptions are trips limited to Nairobi city, most coastal counties, or the northeastern counties of Mandera, Wajir and Garissa. So if you're going on safari to game parks outside those areas, plan on getting it [1].

The CDC also recommends:
- Routine shots: be up to date on MMR (measles, mumps, rubella), polio, Tdap/Td, chickenpox, flu, shingles and COVID-19 [1].
- Hepatitis A and typhoid: for most travelers [1].
- Hepatitis B: for unvaccinated travelers under 60 [1].
- Situational vaccines to discuss with a clinician: rabies (common in dogs there), cholera (for areas with active outbreaks), and mpox (if you expect sexual contact with new partners or large public events) [1].

Kenya also has malaria, and there's no vaccine for travelers. You'll need prescription antimalarial pills for areas below 2,500 m, which covers most safari and beach destinations. Central Nairobi only calls for insect precautions [1].

Try to see a travel clinic 4–6 weeks before you leave, because some vaccines take time or need more than one dose. Entry rules can also change, so check the CDC Kenya page again close to your departure date. I couldn't load Kenya's Ministry of Health page to confirm directly.

q: What do I have to keep in mind while camping in the wild?
answer:
The first thing to check is whether it's even legal where you're going, because the rules differ a lot from place to place. Scotland lets you wild camp on most unenclosed land under the Scottish Outdoor Access Code, with some exceptions such as the seasonal Camping Management Zones at Loch Lomond & The Trossachs. In most of England and Wales, pitching a tent without the landowner's permission is trespass. Dartmoor is the exception there: the Supreme Court confirmed a right to wild camp on its commons in 2025 [2]. In the US, look up the rules for the specific public land and check for fire bans before you go.

Once you're out there, the Leave No Trace principles are a good guide [1]:
- Plan ahead and tell someone your route and when you expect to be back.
- Pitch your tent on durable ground at least 200 feet (about 70 steps) from lakes and streams, and keep your campsite small.
- Pack out all of your trash.
- For solid human waste, dig a hole 6–8 inches deep at least 200 feet from water, camp and trails, then cover it up.
- Wash dishes and yourself at least 200 feet from water, using only a little biodegradable soap.
- Keep fires small, or use a stove. Store food so animals can't get at it, and don't feed wildlife.

A few practical points on top of that: treat all water from natural sources before drinking it, check the weather forecast, and pack layers, a map and a first-aid kit. Where I live in Scotland the unwritten rule is to stay only two or three nights in one spot [2]. If you tell me where you plan to camp, I can look up the rules for that area.

answer:
It depends a little on the bird, but here's the short version. For wild garden birds, the best foods are close to what they eat in nature: sunflower hearts, peanut granules, nyjer seed, grains, and mealworms. Suet and fat can be put out all year [1]. Good kitchen leftovers include uncooked porridge oats, cake crumbs, grated cheese, and plain cooked pasta [1].

What not to feed:
- **Bread:** It fills birds up but gives them very little nutrition, so it's best avoided [1].
- **Salty or mouldy food:** Skip salted peanuts, salty scraps and anything mouldy [1]. Birds can't get rid of extra salt well, so even a little can be toxic to a small bird [2].
- **Avocado:** It contains a toxin called persin that can cause heart damage, breathing problems and sudden death [2][3].
- **Chocolate and caffeine:** Chocolate, coffee, tea and soda can cause heart-rhythm problems, seizures and death [2][3].
- **Onion and garlic:** These can damage blood cells [3].
- **Fruit pits and seeds:** Pits and seeds from apples, cherries, apricots, plums and peaches contain cyanide [3].
- **Xylitol:** This sweetener is dangerous [3].
- **Dairy:** Avoid large amounts, because birds don't digest lactose well [3].

The toxic-food list comes mostly from pet-bird guidance, but it's worth following for wild birds too. If a pet bird eats something toxic, call a vet right away and don't try to make it vomit [3].

q: How do I fix a squeaky door hinge?
answer:
For a quick fix, spray a liquid lubricant into the seams between the hinge knuckles, then open and close the door a few times so it works in [1].

If the squeak comes back, do the proper fix:
1. Keep the door closed and work on one hinge at a time. If you pull all the pins at once, the door can fall.
2. Put a nail against the bottom of the hinge pin and tap it upward with a hammer until you can pull the pin out [1].
3. Wipe the pin clean. If it's rusty, sand it lightly with 120-grit sandpaper [1].
4. Coat it with a thin layer of machine oil, petroleum jelly or white lithium grease [1].
5. Tap the pin back in from the top and swing the door several times to spread the lubricant [1].

If the hinge still squeaks, tighten any loose hinge screws. A badly worn hinge may need replacing [2].

q: How do I make a sourdough starter from scratch?
answer:
It takes about 1–2 weeks. You need flour, water, a jar and a warm spot. This is the usual method:

1. **Start (day 1):** In a clean jar, mix equal weights of flour and water, for example 50 g each. Whole wheat or rye flour works best at the start because it has more nutrients for wild yeast. Cover the jar loosely and leave it somewhere warm for 24 hours [1]. Filtered water is fine. If your tap water is chlorinated, you can leave it out uncovered for a day first [1].
2. **Feed once a day (days 2–3):** Keep feeding daily. From about day 3, discard most of the starter, then feed what's left with fresh flour and water in equal amounts [1].
3. **Switch to twice a day (day 4 on):** Feed every 12 hours. A typical feeding is 20 g starter with 100 g flour (a mix of rye and all-purpose) and 100 g water [2].

Warmth speeds things up. About 26–29°C (80–85°F) is ideal [2].

**Don't give up on day 3 or 4.** It's common to get a burst of bubbles around day 2 that then dies down. That doesn't mean the starter has died, so just keep feeding [2]. If grey liquid ("hooch") forms on top, stir it back in [2].

**When it's ready:** Usually after 7–14 days [3], it will be bubbly, smell pleasantly sour and rise and fall predictably after each feeding [2]. A good sign is that it roughly doubles within several hours of a feeding. At that point you can bake with it.

q: How do I find out which process is using a port on Linux?
answer:
Use `sudo ss -ltnp 'sport = :8080'` (or `sudo ss -ltnp | grep :8080`). Replace 8080 with your port. The `-l` flag shows listening sockets, `-t` limits it to TCP, `-n` shows port numbers instead of service names, and `-p` shows the process name and PID. Use `-u` instead of `-t` for UDP. ss is part of iproute2 and has replaced the older `netstat -tulpn` [1][3].

You can also use `sudo lsof -i :8080`, which lists the command, PID and user for anything that has that port open [3][2]. Another option is `sudo fuser -v 8080/tcp`, which comes from the psmisc package. `fuser -k 8080/tcp` will kill whatever is holding the port [1][2].

Run these with sudo. Without root you only see details for your own processes, so the process column may be empty for anything owned by root or another user [1]. If ss shows nothing but the port is still taken, check whether it's held by a container or a different network namespace.

q: How do I fix a flat bike tyre when I'm out on a ride?
answer:
Most riders swap in a spare inner tube at the roadside and patch the punctured one later at home, because swapping is much faster [1][2].

1. Get the wheel off. Shift into the smallest rear cog so the chain is slack, and open your rim brake if you have one. Then open the quick-release lever or unscrew the thru-axle and drop the wheel out [1].
2. Take out the tube. Push a tyre lever under one edge of the tyre (the bead) and pry it over the rim. Slide the lever around the wheel until that whole side is free. Push the valve out through the rim and pull the tube out [1].
3. Find what caused it. Run your fingers carefully around the inside of the tyre and look at the tread. Pick out any glass, thorn or grit. If you skip this, the same object will puncture the new tube straight away [1][3].
4. Fit the new tube. Put a little air in it so it holds its shape. Push the valve through the rim hole first, then tuck the tube into the tyre [1].
5. Refit the tyre. Work the bead back onto the rim with your thumbs, starting at the valve and finishing there. Try not to use levers for the last tight section, because that's how you pinch and puncture the new tube [1].
6. Check and inflate. Make sure the tyre is sitting evenly all the way around and no tube is poking out under the bead. Then pump it up, refit the wheel and close your brake again [1].

If you don't have a spare, you can patch the hole where you are. Self-adhesive patches are quicker at the roadside, but patches you glue on are more likely to last [3]. It's worth carrying a spare tube, tyre levers, patches and a mini pump or CO2 inflator on every ride [2][4].

q: How do I get rid of black mould in the bathroom for good?
answer:
To get rid of black mould for good, you need to deal with the damp that feeds it, not just the stain. Otherwise it keeps coming back.

Getting it off: On hard surfaces like tiles, grout and painted walls, scrub with detergent and water, then dry the area completely. The US EPA says you don't need to use bleach as a routine cleaner for mould [1][2]. If you do use bleach, never mix it with ammonia or other cleaners, because that creates toxic fumes. Mould that has grown into silicone sealant or crumbling grout usually can't be cleaned out, so cut it out and redo it. If the mouldy patch is bigger than about 10 square feet (roughly 1 m²), or keeps coming back through the plaster, get a professional in [2].

Keeping it away: Keep the room's humidity below 60%, ideally 30–50% [2]. Run the extractor fan while you shower and for at least 15 minutes afterwards, and open a window or leave the door open when you can [3]. Squeegee or wipe the walls and screen after each shower, dry towels somewhere else, and fix any leaks quickly [3]. The EPA says that more ventilation plus more frequent cleaning usually stops bathroom mould from returning [2].

If it still keeps coming back, check whether the fan actually pulls air out. Also look for a cold external wall or a hidden leak, since those are the usual causes.

q: How do I solve a quadratic equation by completing the square?
answer:
The idea is to rewrite the left side as a perfect square, (x + something)², and then take square roots [1][2].

**Steps:**
1. Move the constant term to the right side. If the x² term has a coefficient other than 1, divide every term by it [1].
2. Take the coefficient of x, halve it (keeping its sign), and square the result. Add that number to both sides [1][3].
3. The left side now factors as (x + half the coefficient)² [2].
4. Take the square root of both sides. Remember to include ±. Then solve for x [1][3].

**Example:** x² + 6x − 7 = 0
- Move the constant: x² + 6x = 7.
- Half of 6 is 3, and 3² = 9, so add 9 to both sides: x² + 6x + 9 = 16.
- Factor: (x + 3)² = 16.
- Take square roots: x + 3 = ±4, so x = 1 or x = −7.

If the right side comes out negative, there are no real solutions. If you do this with the general equation ax² + bx + c = 0, you get the quadratic formula. You can use this method even when the quadratic doesn't factor nicely [1][3].

q: What is surströmming, and why does it smell so bad?
answer:
Surströmming is a Swedish dish of fermented Baltic Sea herring that goes back at least to the 16th century. It's a different thing from ordinary pickled herring. The fish are soaked in strong brine to draw out the blood, then moved to a weaker brine and fermented for at least six months. They're canned in early July, and they keep fermenting inside the sealed cans [1]. By tradition, the new season's catch can't be sold before the third Thursday in August. People usually eat it outdoors on thin flatbread with potatoes and red onion [1].

The smell comes from what the fermentation produces. Enzymes in the fish and salt-tolerant Halanaerobium bacteria break the fish down into several compounds [1][2][3]:
- Hydrogen sulfide, which smells like rotten eggs
- Butyric acid, which smells like rancid butter or vomit
- Propionic acid, which is part of what makes body odor smell
- Acetic acid, the sharp note in vinegar

The bacteria also make carbon dioxide. That's why the cans visibly bulge, which is normal for surströmming. The trapped gas is also why the smell is strongest the moment you open a can [1][2]. It isn't actually rotten, though. When scientists analyze it, they don't find the typical decay chemicals like putrescine, cadaverine or skatole [2].

q: What happened during the dancing plague of 1518?
answer:
In July 1518, in Strasbourg (then part of the Holy Roman Empire, now in France), a woman named Frau Troffea stepped into the street and started dancing and couldn't stop. She kept going for days, and within about a week more than 30 people had joined her. By August, estimates put the number of dancers somewhere between 50 and 400. [1][2] Accounts describe people dancing until their feet were raw and bloody and they collapsed from exhaustion. [3]

The city's first response made things worse. Believing the dancers needed to dance the fever out of their systems, officials opened guildhalls, hired musicians, and brought in strong men to hold the dancers up. When the outbreak kept growing, they reversed course: they banned public dancing and then music, and sent the afflicted to a shrine of Saint Vitus. There the dancers were given crosses and red shoes sprinkled with holy water. [1][2] By early September the outbreak had died down. [1]

Some later accounts say as many as 15 people a day died, but the surviving records from Strasbourg at the time don't mention any deaths, so historians still argue over whether anyone died. [1] The cause isn't known for sure. One old theory is ergot poisoning from moldy grain. Historian John Waller argues instead that it was a stress-induced mass psychogenic illness, brought on by famine and disease in a population that believed an angry Saint Vitus could curse people with dancing. [1][4]

q: What was the Antikythera mechanism used for?
answer:
The Antikythera mechanism was a hand-cranked Greek astronomical calculator, often called the first analog computer. It dates to around the late 2nd or early 1st century BCE and was recovered in 1901 from a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera [1][2].

When you turned the handle, its bronze gears showed where the Sun, the Moon and probably the planets were in the sky. It also showed the Moon's phase and could predict eclipses decades in advance [2][3]. On the back, one spiral dial used the Babylonian 223-month Saros cycle to predict eclipses. Another followed the 19-year Metonic cycle that lines up lunar months with the solar year [2][4].

It also worked as a calendar. A small dial inside the Metonic one tracked the four-year cycle of the Panhellenic games, including the Olympics [1][2]. Put simply, it was a mechanical model of the Greek cosmos and calendar, probably used for teaching, showing off, or scientific or religious timekeeping. No one knows for sure who owned it or exactly how they used it.

q: Why isn't it Sydney?
answer:
It comes down to the rivalry between Sydney and Melbourne. When the colonies federated in 1901, those were the two biggest cities, and neither would accept the other as the national capital [1]. The compromise went into section 125 of the Constitution. The capital had to be in a federal territory inside New South Wales but at least 100 miles (about 160 km) from Sydney, and Parliament would sit in Melbourne until the new seat of government was ready [2][1]. The Yass–Canberra district was picked in 1908, so Canberra was essentially a purpose-built, neutral city [1]. Parliament finally moved from Melbourne to Canberra and opened in the Provisional Parliament House on 9 May 1927 [3].

q: And what went wrong at Chernobyl?
answer:
At Chernobyl, a flawed reactor design combined with a badly run safety test. In the early hours of 26 April 1986, operators at Unit 4 were testing whether the turbine could keep the cooling pumps running for a short time after a power loss as it spun down. To run the test, they switched off safety systems and pulled out most of the control rods. That left the reactor in an unstable state at low power, made worse by a buildup of xenon, a byproduct that absorbs neutrons [1].

The Soviet RBMK design had a "positive void coefficient." In most reactors, when cooling water turns to steam, the chain reaction slows down. In this one it sped up, because steam absorbs fewer neutrons than water does. So once the water started boiling, the extra steam raised power, which made more steam, and the reaction ran away [1][2]. When operators tried an emergency shutdown, the control rods made things worse. Because of how their tips were designed, pushing them in briefly increased power before it could fall [1][3]. Soviet experts had known about both flaws for years, but the information was classified and the fixes were never made [3].

Power spiked to about 100 times the normal level. A steam explosion blew off the reactor's 1,000-tonne lid, and a second explosion followed. The reactor had no strong containment building to hold anything in, and the graphite in its core caught fire, releasing radioactive material for about 10 days. Two workers died in the explosions, and about 28 more died of radiation sickness within weeks [1].
